files.lesson.md: --- order: 6 unit: circles node: AC9M7M03 n1 title: Parts of a circle summary: "Every point of a circle is the same distance from its centre: the radius. The diameter goes right across through the centre, two radii long (d = 2r). A chord joins any two points; the circumference is the distance all the way round." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "Wheels, plates, clocks and pizza: why does a wheel roll smoothly? Because every point on its edge is the same distance from the axle." app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8278 url: http://127.0.0.1:8278/index.html readySelector: "#sl-r" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: circle.yml#explain-pic, caption: "Centre, radius (3 cm), diameter (6 cm: two radii), a chord, and the circumference all the way round." } explainClip: query: { code: "@circle.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "Radius and diameter" say: "The diameter is two radii." clip: - caption: { text: "The radius: from the centre to the edge.", say: "The radius goes from the centre to the edge." } - wait: 1000 - caption: { text: "The diameter: right across, through the centre.", say: "The diameter goes right across, through the centre." } - wait: 1000 - click: Make the radius bigger - click: Make the radius bigger - caption: { text: "Radius 4, diameter 8: always two radii.", say: "Radius four, diameter eight. Always two radii." } - expect: { selector: "#gsum", contains: "diameter 8" } - wait: 1400 --- A **circle** is every point the same distance from one point, its **centre**. That distance is the **radius** ($r$). A line right across the circle, through the centre, is the **diameter** ($d$). ## Predict: radius 5 ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to a diameter for radius 5 shows whether they know the diameter is two radii, or halve, or mix the two up." check: type: predict q: "A circle has radius 5 cm. What is its diameter?" options: ["10 cm", "2.5 cm", "5 cm", "25 cm"] actual: "10 cm: the diameter goes from the edge, through the centre, to the other edge: two radii. 2.5 halves the radius." ``` Picture a radius, then another one pointing the opposite way. ## Run: diameter 10 ```step stage: run insight: "Changing the radius until the diameter is 10 shows the diameter is always twice the radius." try: { playground: board, starter: "circle.yml#run", height: 540 } check: { type: board, text: "Make a circle with diameter 10 cm. What is its radius? Was your prediction right?", when: "d = 10", explain: "Radius 5 cm: 10 = 2 × 5." } ``` Watch the radius and the diameter as the circle grows. The board was showing how they fit together. The diameter is two radii: $d = 2r$, so $r = d \div 2$. Two more words: - A **chord** is a straight line joining any two points on the circle. The diameter is the longest chord. - The **circumference** ($C$) is the distance all the way round: the circle's perimeter. ## Investigate: the parts ```step stage: investigate insight: "Each part has its own job; Jay calls the diameter the radius. Every diameter is a chord, but only chords through the centre are diameters." tasks: - check: type: match q: "Match each part of a circle to what it is." pairs: - ["radius", "from the centre to the edge"] - ["diameter", "right across, through the centre"] - ["chord", "a straight line joining two points on the circle"] - ["circumference", "the distance all the way round"] explain: "The radius is half the diameter; the diameter is the longest chord; the circumference is the perimeter." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#jay" text: "Jay works out how far a chair at the edge of a round table is from its centre. Click the line where he goes wrong." answer: 2 fault: logic misconception: radius-diameter explain: "Line 2: across through the centre is the diameter. The radius is half of it: 120 ÷ 2 = 60 cm." - check: type: question q: "Is every chord a diameter?" options: ["No: only a chord that passes through the centre is a diameter", "Yes: they both go across the circle", "No: a chord is always curved"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "A chord near the edge goes across but misses the centre: it is shorter.", "A chord is straight; the circumference is the curved part."] explain: "Every diameter is a chord (the longest one), but most chords miss the centre." ``` ### Two radii make a diameter Here are the relationships. ```worked d = 2r :: The diameter is two radii, end to end through the centre. r = 5 \Rightarrow d = 2 \times 5 = 10 :: Radius to diameter: double. d = 120 \Rightarrow r = 120 \div 2 = 60 :: Diameter to radius: halve. C :: The circumference is the distance round; the next lessons find it from d. ``` Now match the parts. ### Find the mistake Read Jay's working. Which part goes right across? ### Chords ## Modify: one change at a time ```step stage: modify insight: "One change at a time: an odd diameter on the board (a half radius), diameter to radius, radius to diameter with a decimal, then the longest chord and two radii in a line." try: { playground: board, starter: "circle.yml#halves", height: 540 } tasks: - starter: "circle.yml#halves" hint: "The radius is half of 7." check: { type: board, text: "Make a circle with diameter 7 cm.", when: "d = 7", explain: "Radius 3.5 cm: 2 × 3.5 = 7." } - check: type: answer q: "A bike wheel has diameter 18 inches. What is its radius, in inches?" answer: "9" feedback: - ["36", "That doubles. The radius is half the diameter."] explain: "18 ÷ 2 = 9 inches." - check: type: answer q: "A circle has radius 4.5 cm. What is its diameter, in cm?" answer: "9" feedback: - ["2.25", "That halves. The diameter is two radii."] explain: "2 × 4.5 = 9 cm." - check: type: question q: "Edge case: two radii point in exactly opposite directions from the centre. Together they make a…" options: ["diameter", "chord that misses the centre", "circumference", "radius twice as long"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "They pass through the centre.", "They are straight, not round.", "A radius always ends at the centre."] explain: "End to end through the centre: a diameter, d = 2r." ``` ### Diameter 7 Each task changes one thing. ### Diameter to radius ### Radius to diameter ### Opposite radii ## Practise: circle parts ```step stage: practise insight: "Doubling, halving and the words, mixed; mixing up radius and diameter is the planted slip; the review keeps volume fresh." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "A clock face has radius 12 cm. What is its diameter, in cm?" answer: "24" feedback: - ["6", "That halves."] explain: "2 × 12 = 24 cm." - check: type: answer q: "A coin has diameter 3 cm. What is its radius, in cm?" answer: "1.5" feedback: - ["6", "That doubles."] explain: "3 ÷ 2 = 1.5 cm." smaller: check: { type: number, q: "Say a circle has radius 4 cm. Two radii, end to end through the centre, make a line right across it. How long is that line, in cm?", answer: 8, tolerance: 0, explain: "4 + 4 = 8 cm. That line is the diameter, so the diameter is bigger than the radius." } - check: type: question q: "What is the longest chord of a circle?" options: ["A diameter", "A radius", "The circumference", "Any chord near the edge"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "A radius stops at the centre, so it is not a chord.", "The circumference is curved, not a chord.", "Chords near the edge are short."] explain: "A chord through the centre, the diameter, is the longest." - check: type: answer q: "Review: a box is 2 cm by 3 cm by 4 cm. What is its volume, in cm³?" answer: "24" feedback: - ["9", "That adds."] explain: "2 × 3 × 4 = 24 cm³." ``` ### Double ### Halve ### Longest chord ### Review: volume ## Make: the biggest circle in a box ```step stage: make insight: "Fitting the biggest circle in a rectangle means reasoning about the diameter against the shorter side, then halving for the radius." hint: ["The circle must fit across the narrow way.", "Its diameter can be at most the shorter side."] check: type: reasoning q: "A box lid is a rectangle 10 cm by 6 cm. What is the radius of the biggest circle that fits flat inside it? Write your reasons." steps: - ["The diameter can be at most 6 cm", "the circle must fit across the shorter side"] - ["$r = 6 \\div 2 = 3$ cm", "the radius is half the diameter"] picks: - step: 1 options: ["The circle must fit across the shorter side", "The circle must fit along the longer side", "The circle's diameter is the perimeter of the box"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "A 10 cm circle would stick out of the 6 cm sides.", "The diameter is a straight distance across the circle."] answer: "3" feedback: - ["5", "A diameter of 10 cm would not fit across the 6 cm side."] - ["6", "6 cm is the diameter. The radius is half."] explain: "The diameter is limited by the 6 cm side, so r = 3 cm." ``` Then: how many of those circles fit side by side in the lid? ## Make: a round table, on paper ```step stage: make insight: "A table with room to pull out chairs is a circle inside a bigger circle with the same centre: the clear space is added to the radius, on every side." hint: ["Draw the table, then a bigger circle round it with the same centre.", "The 0.5 m is added to the radius, or twice to the diameter."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A round table has a diameter of 1.2 m. It stands in the middle of a square room, and people need 0.5 m clear all round the table to pull out a chair. What is the smallest width the room can be, in metres?" steps: - ["Sketch the table and a bigger circle round it, 0.5 m out, with the same centre", "the clear space goes all the way round"] - ["$r = 1.2 \\div 2 = 0.6$ m, so the big circle has $r = 0.6 + 0.5 = 1.1$ m", "the clear space is added to the radius"] - ["$d = 2 \\times 1.1 = 2.2$ m", "the room must be as wide as the big circle's diameter"] picks: - step: 2 q: "How does the 0.5 m get into the working?" options: - "It is on every side: add it to the radius, then double (or add it to the diameter twice)" - "Add it once to the diameter: 1.2 + 0.5" - "Add it to the radius and stop: the room is 1.1 m wide" answer: 0 feedback: [null, "That leaves out the space on the other side of the table.", "1.1 m is the radius of the big circle. The room is as wide as its diameter."] answer: "2.2" tolerance: 0 feedback: - ["1.7", "That adds the 0.5 m once. There is clear space on both sides of the table."] - ["1.1", "That is the radius of the big circle. The room must be as wide as its diameter."] criteria: - "I drew the table and the clear space as two circles with the same centre." - "I changed between radius and diameter the right way each time." - "My answer is bigger than the table's 1.2 m." explain: "The table's radius is 0.6 m, so the big circle has radius 0.6 + 0.5 = 1.1 m and diameter 2.2 m. The room is at least 2.2 m wide." ``` Do this one in your book, not on the screen. The table and the room are made up for the task. Sketch the two circles, work out the room's width, and type it. **Also used in** - **Wheels.** A bike wheel rolls smoothly because every point on its rim is the same distance from the axle: the radius. - **Farm circles.** From the air, farms in dry country are green circles, watered by an arm turning about a centre. The arm is a radius. - **Pizza.** A pizza is sold by its diameter, but how much you get depends on the radius. The area lessons come back to this. ```teacher summary: Students name the parts of a circle (centre, radius, diameter, chord, circumference), use d = 2r in both directions, and reason about the biggest circle that fits a rectangle (AC9M7M03, node 1). time: 35 timing: Predict and Run 6 min · Investigate 10 min · Modify 8 min · Practise and Make 11 min goals: - I can name the parts of a circle. - I can find the diameter from the radius, and the radius from the diameter. - I can explain why the diameter is the longest chord. struggle: Keeping radius and diameter apart in word problems. Ask students to sketch the circle and mark the given length on it before they double or halve. before: > Do the Run board yourself first. Students meet these words informally in primary school; this lesson makes them exact. The one idea: the radius is centre to edge; the diameter is two radii right across; d = 2r. The common mistake is mixing them up in context (Jay's mistake). Circumference is named here and found in the next two lessons. running: - "Predict: students who chose 2.5 halved the radius." - "Run: ask what stays true as the circle grows." - "Investigate: draw a chord near the edge and one through the centre; compare lengths." - "Modify: for diameter 7, ask why the radius is not a whole number." - "Make: let students sketch the lid before answering." - "Paper: the round table is worked in books. Books out; look at the sketch of two circles with the same centre, not the screen, and ask who added the 0.5 m only once." stuck: - see: A student calls the diameter the radius (Jay's mistake). ask: Does it stop at the centre or go right across? fix: Centre to edge is the radius; edge to edge through the centre is the diameter. - see: A student doubles when they should halve. ask: Is the diameter bigger or smaller than the radius? fix: "The diameter is bigger: double the radius; halve the diameter." - see: A student thinks the circumference is a chord. ask: Is it straight or curved? fix: The circumference is the curved distance round. stretch: How many 3 cm radius coasters fit, in a grid, on a 30 cm by 24 cm tray? support: Use a paper circle folded in half (the fold is a diameter) and in quarters (the centre). leads: | Next: Discovering π (node 2): how the circumference compares to the diameter. Where it leads: circle theorems (Year 10), and the area of a circle (Year 8). exit: q: A circular pond has diameter 9 m. Find its radius. What is a chord? a: 4.5 m. A straight line joining two points on the circle. explain: > A **circle** is all the points the same distance (the **radius**, $r$) from its **centre**. - The **diameter** ($d$) goes right across through the centre: $d = 2r$, and $r = d \div 2$. - A **chord** joins any two points; the diameter is the longest chord. - The **circumference** ($C$) is the distance all the way round. ```

# Jay's working for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the wrong line, nothing runs.

# region: jay
A round table is 120 cm across, measured through the centre.
The distance across through the centre is the radius.
So the radius is 120 cm.
A chair at the edge is 120 cm from the centre.
# endregion
